title: A review of cutting tool materials in metal cutting processes
abstract: Abstract Cutting tool material selection plays an influential role in the performance, precision, and economic viability of metal-cutting operations. This article presents a comprehensive review of current and emerging cutting tool materials, examining their properties, applications, and limitations. The discussion covers widely used options such as high-speed steels, ceramics, cemented carbides, cermets, polycrystalline diamond (PCD), and cubic boron nitride (CBN), along with promising next-generation materials. Emphasis is placed on key performance attributes, including hardness, wear resistance, thermal conductivity, and fracture toughness, which directly influence tool life, surface quality, and machining productivity. Developments in surface engineering, particularly in physical vapour deposition (PVD), chemical vapour deposition (CVD), and advanced nano-composite coatings, are also addressed, highlighting their role in enhancing tool performance under challenging cutting conditions. By reviewing machining studies across different alloys, the work identifies persistent challenges, including tool degradation at high cutting speeds, processing of hard-to-machine materials, and cost optimization. The review concludes by outlining future directions for material innovation to improve efficiency, sustainability, and competitiveness in modern manufacturing. An integrated review of cutting tool materials, surface engineering, wear mechanisms, cost considerations, and intelligent tools is presented. The review further presents a mechanistic analysis of abrasive, adhesive, diffusion, and oxidative wear, linking tool composition and coating architecture to degradation behaviour under extreme machining conditions.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The pursuit of high profits, productivity, and tight dimensional tolerances in metal machining has driven the need for continuous changes in hard coatings. The ultimate goal of an effective coating is to maintain most of the required properties at high levels simultaneously. High hardness resists wear; high chemical and thermal stability reduces wear from disintegration and maintains physical properties at high temperatures. High strength prevents nearby rupture at the cutting edge during machining, low friction reduces cutting power, and excellent adherence to the substrate ensures surface protection under substantial cutting loads. It was found that conventional cutting tool materials cannot achieve all desirable properties and are therefore at the highest level [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]. Therefore, compound or advanced cutting tool materials are increasingly of interest.

A significant feature of the modern manufacturing industry is the development of upgraded production processes and cutting tools. The cutting tool plays a pivotal role in any metal-cutting operation. Over the years, many researchers and practitioners have developed a variety of tools and materials. Progress has been made from carbon tool steels to ceramics and diamonds. The key characteristics of the ideal material include toughness, stiffness, friction, wear resistance, high-temperature hardness, specific heat capacity, thermal conductivity, ease of fabrication, and cost. Figure  1  shows the schematic classification of cutting tool materials and surface engineering technologies.
Fig. 1 Schematic classification of cutting tool materials and surface engineering technologies [ 9 ,  10 ,  80 ,  92 ,  96 ]

From a comparative perspective, cutting tool materials exhibit distinct combinations of hardness, thermal stability, fracture toughness, and wear resistance, which govern their suitability for different machining applications. High-speed steels offer superior fracture toughness and shock resistance but have limited hot hardness, which restricts their use to low and moderate cutting speeds. Cemented carbides (WC–Co) provide a balanced combination of hardness and toughness with good thermal conductivity, making them the most versatile and widely adopted tool materials in industrial machining. Ceramic and cermet tools exhibit higher hardness and thermal stability than carbides; however, their relatively low fracture toughness limits their performance under interrupted cutting or vibration-prone conditions. In contrast, superhard materials such as CBN and PCD possess exceptional hardness and wear resistance, enabling high-speed and hard machining. Still, their inherent brittleness and cost necessitate careful, application-specific deployment. This qualitative comparison highlights the trade-offs to consider when selecting cutting tool materials for specific machining environments. sections.heading: Literature search methodology
paragraphs: A systematic literature review was conducted using major databases, including Scopus, Web of Science, Elsevier, Springer Nature, Taylor & Francis, and Google Scholar, for additional sources. Keywords related to machining, cutting tools, tool wear, coatings, and tool materials, etc. were employed. The study considered publications from 1990 to 2025, focusing on peer-reviewed journal articles in English. Following screening and eligibility evaluation, a total of 104 relevant papers were included, as illustrated in Fig.  2 .
Fig. 2 Schematic representation of the literature selection process

sections.heading: High-speed steel (HSS)
paragraphs: This tool material is high-carbon steel, to which the various alloying elements (Chromium, Cobalt, Molybdenum, Vanadium, and Tungsten) have been added in large amounts as compared to alloy tool steels, to improve hardness, toughness, and wear resistance properties. These materials are deep-hardening and can be quenched in oil, air, or salt. They retain their hardness up to 600 °C and can be operated at much higher cutting speeds than alloy tool steels; hence the name “high-speed steel”. Cheung et al. [ 11 ] investigated the impact of advanced preparation on the wear resistance and tool life of HSS drills.

sections.heading: Non-ferrous cast alloys (stellite)
paragraphs: Stellite was introduced in 1915 and is an alloy of Cobalt, Chromium, and Tungsten. Cast metal tools can be shaped into any desired form. Cast alloys bridge the gap between HSS. and carbides. This material exhibits good wear resistance and maintains its hardness at high temperatures, but is less tough than HSS and is sensitive to shock loading. It is recommended for deep-roughing applications at higher speeds and feed rates. It can machine more difficult materials, including stainless steels, high-tensile steels, heat-resistant steels, and C.I. This material is used at surface speeds above those of HSS but below those of carbides, and can withstand cutting temperatures up to 900 °C [ 12 ].

sections.heading: Sintered or cemented carbides
paragraphs: The first sintered carbide cutting tool (tungsten carbide) was marketed in 1926. Since then, extensive research has been conducted, and numerous sintered carbide materials have been developed to improve their performance. Powder metallurgy produces sintered carbides that exhibit extremely high wear resistance and red hardness, as well as high thermal conductivity, low thermal expansion, and high modulus of elasticity. Sohrabpoor et al. [ 13 ] used a carbide cutting insert for turning AISI 4340. Moreover, Wang et al. [ 14 ] used an uncoated carbide tool in high-speed milling and employed a factorial design. Aurich et al. [ 15 ] cemented a carbide tool during the cryogenic turning of AISI 347. Moreover, the effect of cemented carbide tool wear on surface quality during finish turning of Inconel 718 alloy was examined by Jafarian et al. [ 16 ]. Santos et al. [ 17 ] used a cemented carbide insert when turning aluminium alloys under various cutting conditions. Thakur et al. [ 18 ] examined how post-treatments affected the performance of tungsten carbide (K20) tools during the turning of Inconel 718. They discovered that treated tools yield a superior machined surface finish than untreated tools.

sections.heading: Ceramics and oxides
paragraphs: Ceramics or sintered oxides were developed as cutting tool materials during 1950–1960. These materials contain aluminium oxide (Al 2 O 3 ) with additions such as Cr 2 O 3 , NiO, MgO, TiC, TiO, etc., to enhance grain structure, cutting characteristics, and sintering. Ceramic tool materials offer higher abrasion resistance, are tougher than cemented carbides and HSS, and have less of a tendency to weld to metals during machining than cemented carbides and HSS. However, due to their relatively low fracture toughness and limited resistance to impact loading, ceramic tools are highly susceptible to catastrophic brittle fracture under interrupted cutting, vibration, or thermo-mechanical shock conditions. These materials are particularly successful for machining cast iron and high-tensile materials, at cutting speeds 2 to 3 times those of cemented carbides. In a dry environment, Das et al. [ 19 ] tested the machining of hardened AISI 4140 steel with a TiN-coated ceramic tool. Davoudinejad and Noordin [ 20 ] investigated the impact of cutting-edge preparation on tool characteristics while using ceramic tools to hard-turn DF-3 tool steel.

sections.heading: Cermets
paragraphs: The cermets are made out of ceramics and metals that have been fused in the same way as powder metallurgy components are made. They combine the toughness and thermal shock resistance of metals with the high refractoriness of ceramics. In dry machining, Canteli et al. [ 21 ] focused on the cutting characteristics of novel TiCN-HSS cermets. When the cermets inserts were compared with commercial HSS inserts, tool life increased dramatically.

sections.heading: Laminated and coated carbides
paragraphs: It is well known that the addition of TiC can increase the resistance of straight tungsten carbide to crater wear. Laminates consisting of a hard, thin TiC surface layer in the form of throw-away tips are attached to the rake face of a WC tip body by epoxy resin in laminated carbides. These tools resist the diffusive wear on the crater and give a tough, shock-resistant tool.

Selvaraj et al. [ 22 ] used carbide inserts coated with TiC and TiCN in dry turning. Shao et al. [ 23 ] used a sintered carbide K10 coating with TiN and TiCN for high-speed milling of Mar-247 under orthogonal cutting conditions. Breidenstein and Denkena [ 24 ] analyzed the characteristics of PVD-coated carbide-cutting tools. Chakraborty et al. [ 25 ] used carbide inserts coated with PVD TiALN-TiN in both semi-dry and dry machining. They found that high levels of diffusion wear occur during dry machining. In dry and high-speed machining of hardened steel, Pal et al. [ 26 ] studied the performance of CVD-coated carbide tools. Under dry and lubricated circumstances, Ucun et al. [ 27 ] assessed the performance of coated and uncoated WC-Co tools for the micro-milling of 718 nickel superalloy. Compared with the uncoated tools, the coated tools exhibited less wear.

sections.heading: Cubic boron nitride (CBN)
paragraphs: When compared to diamond, CBN has a greater hardness and thermal conductivity, as well as substantially higher tensile strength. For machining steel, CBN is utilized as a replacement for diamond since it is chemically inert. Other applications include the use of a grinding wheel on HSS tools for machining high-temperature alloys, such as Nimonic, titanium, Stainless steel, Stellite, and Chilled cast iron. In dealing with iron-based alloys and hardened steels, the life of a CBN tool is 4 to 5 times higher than that of a diamond tool. Compared with ceramic tool materials, PCBN cutting tool materials offer greater hardness, superior abrasion resistance, and outstanding strength retention at both high and low temperatures [ 28 ]. CBN, comparable Sialon, and whisker-reinforced ceramic tools now cost more than 10 times as much as commercially coated cemented carbide tools, despite their overall performance appearing superior to that of cemented carbide tools [ 29 ]. When machining hardened bearing steels, Sahin [ 30 ] examined the tool life of ceramic and cubic boron nitride (CBN) cutting tools. The performance of the CBN cutting tool was superior to that of the ceramic-based cutting tool. Sobiyi et al. [ 28 ] examined hard turning of martensitic stainless steel using mixed-ceramic and CBN tools. They observed good dimensional accuracy produced by CBN tools.

Despite their superior hot hardness, abrasion resistance, and thermal stability, CBN cutting tools exhibit several limitations that restrict their widespread industrial adoption. The most significant constraint is the high capital cost associated with CBN tool fabrication, which limits their economic viability to high-value or high-volume machining operations. In addition, CBN tools are inherently brittle, making them susceptible to edge chipping and fracture under interrupted cutting conditions, vibration, or mechanical shock. Although CBN is chemically more stable than diamond when machining ferrous alloys, chemical wear and diffusion-related degradation can still occur at elevated cutting temperatures, particularly during high-speed or dry machining. These limitations necessitate careful process planning and restrict the use of CBN tools to specific applications, such as hard turning of hardened steels under controlled machining conditions.

sections.heading: PCD
paragraphs: The hardest of all the cutting tool materials is diamond. Extreme hardness, minimal thermal expansion, excellent heat conductivity, and an extremely low coefficient of friction are all characteristics of a diamond. When a high level of surface polish and dimensional precision is required, this is the method to utilize. Diamond tools are fragile and have low shock resistance; thus, they should be handled carefully. Tough, abrasive non-ferrous materials, plastics, ceramics, and glass have all been successfully machined using polycrystalline diamonds. The material can also be used by bonding its thin layer to a WC substrate. A WC coating that is tougher than diamond will increase the tool’s shock resistance. Kumar and Chauhan [ 31 ] used a polycrystalline diamond tool to evaluate the effects of cutting parameters on surface roughness during the turning of an AL 7075 hard ceramic composite (PCD).

Many studies comparing the performance of PCD to other tool materials have been published. Ji et al. [ 32 ] experimentally assessed polycrystalline diamond (PCD) tool geometries for milling titanium alloy at high feed rates. When milling Ti-6Al-4 V at speeds of more than 100 m/min, Oosthuizen et al. [ 33 ] found that a PCD tool had a longer tool life than a coated carbide tool. In addition, Corduan et al. [ 34 ] investigated the wear mechanisms of PCD, PCBN, and TiB2-coated carbide and reported turning results on Ti-6Al-4 V, indicating that a PCD tool performed well. Muguthu and Gao [ 35 ] investigated the performance of PCD, uncoated CBN, and coated CBN tools. They observed that the dominant wear mechanisms among CBN tools are fracture, chipping, abrasion, and adhesion, whereas for PCD tools, they are chipping, abrasion, and adhesion.

Polycrystalline diamond (PCD) tools, while offering exceptional hardness, low friction, and excellent thermal conductivity, also suffer from critical limitations that affect their industrial applicability. One major limitation is their high material and manufacturing cost, which often confines their use to precision machining of non-ferrous materials and abrasive composites. Furthermore, PCD tools are highly brittle, increasing the risk of edge chipping and catastrophic failure during interrupted cuts or under unstable machining conditions. A key drawback of PCD is its chemical reactivity with ferrous materials at elevated temperatures, leading to accelerated tool wear and loss of cutting-edge integrity. Consequently, despite their superior performance in machining aluminum alloys, composites, and ceramics, the adoption of PCD tools in industrial practice remains application-specific and economically selective.

No single material can be considered optimal for achieving the necessary tool properties. The relative relevance of the above parameters will be determined by the nature of the machined product (precision and cost), the production volume, and the type of machining process, such as roughing or finishing (intermittent or continuous, high or low speed). The kind of service to which the tool will be subjected influences its material selection. No substance is superior in every way; instead, each has its own set of properties that restrict its range of applicability. Table  2  shows an overview of known cutting tool materials.

sections.heading: Chemical composition–thermo-mechanical property correlation of cutting tool materials
paragraphs: For WC–Co cemented carbides, the revised manuscript now explains the role of WC grain size and cobalt binder content in determining the hardness–toughness trade-off. Grain refinement enhances hardness and abrasion resistance via grain-boundary strengthening, whereas increased Co content improves fracture toughness but reduces hot hardness due to binder softening at elevated temperatures [ 77 ,  78 ]. The effect of cobalt diffusion and high-temperature degradation mechanisms has also been discussed. For oxide and nitride ceramics (Al 2 O 3  and Si 3 N 4 ), the analysis now links strong ionic–covalent bonding to superior retention of hot hardness, oxidation resistance, and chemical stability above 1000 °C [ 79 ]. The elongated grain morphology in Si3N4-based ceramics, which promotes crack deflection and improved fracture resistance, has also been elaborated.

In the case of superhard materials, the bonding structure of CBN and PCD has been correlated with their thermo-mechanical behavior. CBN exhibits excellent thermal stability and chemical inertness during ferrous machining, making it suitable for hard-turning applications [ 80 ]. Despite its extremely high hardness and thermal conductivity, PCD undergoes diffusion wear during machining of ferrous alloys due to the solubility of carbon in iron at elevated temperatures [ 80 ].

The revised manuscript also critically evaluates the effect of alloying elements in advanced coatings. The addition of aluminium in TiAlN coatings promotes the formation of protective Al 2 O 3  scales and enhances hot hardness via spinodal decomposition mechanisms [ 81 ]. Similarly, chromium addition to AlCrN coatings improves oxidation resistance by promoting Cr 2 O 3  formation. Nanocomposite architectures further enhance hardness and thermal stability by restricting grain growth and dislocation motion [ 81 ].

Overall, the manuscript now establishes a clear relationship among composition, microstructure, property, and performance, supported by recent literature (2020–2025). This significantly strengthens the scientific depth of the review by linking chemical bonding, phase stability, and alloying strategies to thermo-mechanical performance and wear resistance.

sections.heading: Influence of tool geometry on machining performance
paragraphs: While material composition governs intrinsic thermo-mechanical properties, tool geometry significantly influences stress distribution, heat generation, chip formation, and wear mechanisms during machining. Therefore, optimal tool performance is achieved through the combined optimization of material and geometric parameters.

sections.heading: Rake angle and clearance angle
paragraphs: The rake angle directly affects cutting forces, chip flow, and temperature at the tool–chip interface. Positive rake angles reduce cutting forces and heat generation but may weaken edge strength, particularly in brittle materials such as ceramics and PCBN. Negative rake angles, commonly used for super-hard tools, increase compressive stress at the cutting edge and improve resistance to edge chipping during hard turning [ 82 ,  83 ].

The clearance angle influences flank wear and friction between the tool and the machined surface. Insufficient clearance increases rubbing and temperature, accelerating flank wear, whereas excessive clearance reduces edge strength [ 83 ].

sections.heading: Cutting edge radius and edge preparation
paragraphs: Edge preparation (honing the radius or chamfering) plays a critical role in determining fracture resistance, especially for brittle tool materials. A larger edge radius improves load distribution and reduces stress concentration, thereby enhancing resistance to catastrophic brittle fracture and thermo-mechanical shock. However, excessive edge rounding may increase ploughing forces and energy consumption [ 84 ]. For ceramic and PCBN tools, optimized edge honing significantly improves tool life under interrupted cutting conditions [ 85 ].

sections.heading: Chip breaker geometry
paragraphs: Chip breaker design affects chip curl, segmentation, and evacuation efficiency. Proper chip control reduces heat accumulation and prevents built-up edge formation, particularly when machining ductile materials with coated carbide tools [ 86 ].

sections.heading: Geometry–material interaction
paragraphs: The interaction between geometry and material properties is especially critical for advanced coatings and super-hard materials. For example:

Coated carbides benefit from optimized rake angles to reduce coating delamination stresses. Ceramics require negative rake geometries to maintain compressive stress states. PCD tools require sharp cutting edges for machining non-ferrous materials, but may need reinforced edges for composite machining.

Recent studies emphasize that tool life prediction models must integrate both material properties and geometric parameters to accurately assess performance under high-speed and hard machining conditions [ 82 ,  84 ,  86 ].
Thus, tool geometry should be considered an integral design parameter alongside chemical composition and thermo-mechanical properties when selecting cutting tools.

sections.heading: Quantitative comparison of thermo-mechanical properties
paragraphs: To provide a clearer understanding of performance differences among cutting tool materials, quantitative comparisons of hardness, hot hardness, fracture toughness, thermal conductivity, and applicable cutting speed ranges are presented in Figs.  3 ,  4  and  5 .

sections.heading: Hardness and fracture toughness comparison
paragraphs: Figure  3  illustrates the comparative room-temperature hardness and fracture toughness of major cutting tool materials, including WC–Co carbides, alumina-based ceramics, PCBN, and PCD. While PCD exhibits the highest hardness (> 70 GPa), its fracture toughness is lower than WC–Co carbides. In contrast, cemented carbides demonstrate moderate hardness (15–22 GPa) with superior fracture toughness (8–15 MPa·m½), making them suitable for interrupted cutting operations [ 87 ,  88 ]. This trade-off between hardness and toughness highlights the importance of balanced material selection.
Fig. 3 Hardness comparison of Tool materials [ 10 ,  77 ,  78 ,  79 – 80 ]

sections.heading: Hot hardness retention with temperature
paragraphs: Figure  4  presents the variation of hardness as a function of temperature. Carbides exhibit gradual hardness reduction above 600 °C due to binder softening, whereas CBN and advanced TiAlN-based coatings retain hardness beyond 800–1000 °C due to strong covalent bonding and oxidation-resistant oxide layer formation [ 89 ,  90 ]. The superior hot hardness of PCBN explains its suitability for hard turning of hardened steels at elevated cutting speeds.
Fig. 4 Hot hardness retention with temperatures [ 77 ,  79 ,  80 ,  89 ]

sections.heading: Influence of chemical composition (WC–co system)
paragraphs: Figure  5  shows the effect of cobalt binder content on the hardness and fracture toughness of WC–Co carbides. Increasing Co content enhances fracture toughness but reduces hardness and high-temperature strength due to softening of the metallic binder phase [ 87 ,  88 ,  89 ,  90 – 91 ].
Fig. 5 Effect of co content on WC-Co properties [ 68 ,  77 ,  91 ]

sections.heading: Suitability of tool materials for specific machining operations
paragraphs: The selection of cutting tool materials must be aligned with the specific machining process, workpiece material, cutting speed regime, and loading conditions. Tool suitability is governed not only by intrinsic thermo-mechanical properties but also by wear mechanisms dominant in each machining operation.

sections.heading: Turning and hard turning
paragraphs: For conventional turning of steels at moderate cutting speeds (150–350 m/min), multilayer-coated carbides (e.g., TiAlN, AlCrN) provide an optimal balance among hardness, fracture toughness, and oxidation resistance [ 92 ,  93 ].

In hard turning of hardened steels (> 45 HRC), PCBN tools are preferred due to their superior hot hardness and chemical stability at elevated temperatures. PCBN enables the replacement of grinding in many finishing applications while maintaining dimensional accuracy and surface integrity [ 94 ].

sections.heading: Milling operations
paragraphs: Milling involves intermittent cutting and cyclic mechanical loading. Therefore, fracture toughness and thermal shock resistance are critical. Coated cemented carbides are widely used in general milling due to their balanced mechanical properties [ 92 ].
For high-speed milling of hardened materials, fine-grained PCBN or advanced nanocomposite-coated carbides improve wear resistance and edge stability [ 95 ].

sections.heading: Drilling and hole-making
paragraphs: Drilling generates confined heat and limited chip evacuation. Tools with high thermal conductivity and optimized geometry are preferred. Coated carbides are commonly used for steel drilling. At the same time, PCD tools are particularly well-suited to non-ferrous alloys and abrasive composite materials due to their superior wear resistance and low coefficient of friction [ 96 ].

sections.heading: Machining of superalloys
paragraphs: Nickel-based superalloys generate high cutting temperatures and promote adhesive wear. Advanced ceramic tools (Si 3 N 4 -based) and AlCrN-coated carbides are suitable for high-speed machining of such materials due to improved thermal stability and oxidation resistance [ 93 ,  97 ].

sections.heading: Machining of non-ferrous alloys and composites
paragraphs: PCD tools are highly effective for aluminium, copper, and fibre-reinforced composite materials. Their exceptional hardness and high thermal conductivity reduce built-up edge formation and improve surface finish at very high cutting speeds (up to 3000 m/min) [ 96 ,  98 ].

sections.heading: Surface coating for tooling
paragraphs: An extremely hard surface layer on a low-strength yet robust body is the most desirable attribute in virtually all forms of manufacturing tooling. Mechanical shocks, such as impact loads in interrupted cuts, necessitate toughness. Even in continuous chip manufacturing processes, shocks occur. The following are some of the methods that have been utilized to accomplish this. Table  3  presents critical findings for various cutting-tool materials.

The summarized findings indicate that advanced coating architectures (TiAlN, multilayer PVD/CVD) and surface engineering techniques significantly enhance wear resistance and oxidation stability under high-speed machining conditions. Cryogenic and magnetic field treatments further improve microstructural stability and hardness, thereby extending tool life. Additionally, textured and solid-lubricant-coated tools exhibit reduced friction and adhesive wear, particularly in dry machining environments. Overall, recent studies emphasize that performance improvement is strongly influenced by coating design, substrate composition, and assisted machining techniques.

Fig. 6 Schematic representation of ( a ) monolayer coating, ( b ) multilayer coating architecture, and ( c ) nanocomposite coating structure showing hard nanocrystals embedded in an amorphous matrix [ 7 ,  74 ,  75 – 76 ]

Figure  6  shows the schematic representation of various coating architectures. From a comparative perspective, cutting tool materials exhibit distinct combinations of hardness, thermal stability, fracture toughness, and wear resistance, which govern their suitability for different machining applications. High-speed steels offer superior fracture toughness and shock resistance but have limited hot hardness, which restricts their use to low and moderate cutting speeds. Cemented carbides (WC–Co) provide a balanced combination of hardness and toughness with good thermal conductivity, making them the most versatile and widely adopted tool materials in industrial machining. Ceramic and cermet tools exhibit higher hardness and thermal stability than carbides; however, their relatively low fracture toughness limits their performance under interrupted cutting or vibration-prone conditions. In contrast, superhard materials such as CBN and PCD possess exceptional hardness and wear resistance, enabling high-speed and hard machining, but their inherent brittleness and cost necessitate careful, application-specific deployment. This qualitative comparison highlights the trade-offs to consider when selecting cutting tool materials for specific machining environments.

sections.heading: Hard facing
paragraphs: This is a process for increasing the hardness, strength, and wear resistance of the substrate’s metal by depositing a layer of hard material on it. Bearings, camshafts, valves, hot extrusion dies, hammer mills, stone crushers, shear blades, and a variety of trimming and cutting dies all employ the process. Gas, arc, and shielded arc welding processes are often used for hard facing. The composition of the deposited layer is more consistent with gas and shielded arc welding. Surface using standard arc welding is faster and less expensive, but the risk of dilution of the surfacing metal with the base metal is greater. Hardfacing extends the life of certain components by three or four times and allows worn portions to be repaired several times.

sections.heading: Hard chrome plating
paragraphs: The electrolytic electroplating process is used in the hard chrome plating process. It’s the most popular method for achieving wear resistance. It leads to better lubricant retention and a reduced friction coefficient. The fatigue behaviour of HVOF-sprayed WC–Co coatings and hard chrome plating was compared by Ibrahim and Berndt [ 68 ].

sections.heading: Flame plating
paragraphs: It’s a technique for extending the life of particular cutting instruments and for extreme wear applications. Flame plating has provided the industry with a useful tool for addressing various erosion, abrasion, and wear problems due to the coating’s hard, dense structure. This technique coats a wide range of base metals with a precisely regulated covering of chromium carbide, tungsten carbide, or aluminum oxide. Brass, Copper, Bronze, Cast Iron, Ceramics, Glass, H.S.S., Nickel, Magnesium, Steel, and Titanium, and their Alloys are some of the more frequent materials that have been successfully flame-plated.

sections.heading: Chemical vapour deposition
paragraphs: CVD employs volatile metal compounds that are conveyed as vapours in a gas stream and deposited as metal on any surface that is hot enough to initiate the process. The ability to produce high-density coatings, high-purity materials, high-strength materials, and complex shapes is a major benefit of the CVD method. Medium-temperature CVD is a novel coating method that is particularly useful for multicomponent coatings. It’s being developed to mill ductile iron and stainless steel while also providing better fracture resistance than standard CVD. For Carbide tools, single coatings can be given of Al 2 O 3 , TiC, TiN, HfC, or HfN. Multiple coatings of Al 2 O 3  or TiN can also be given on top of Al 2 O 3  or TiC. Kivak [ 69 ] evaluated the machinability of Hadfield steel with PVD TiAlN- and CVD TiCN/Al2O3-coated carbide inserts under dry-milling conditions, using the Taguchi technique and regression analysis. According to the findings, CVD TiCN/Al2O3-coated carbide inserts outperformed PVD TiAlN-coated carbide inserts in milling Hadfield steel and may be recommended for this application. Davim and Mata [ 70 ] investigated the performance of a diamond-coated tool fabricated by chemical vapour deposition (CVD) when machining PEK composites.

sections.heading: Physical vapour deposition
paragraphs: In the most basic type of PVD, a metal or oxide is vaporized by applying sufficient heat using one of the several processes available. When atoms or molecules interact with the component’s surface, they condense, forming a uniform coating. Because PVD is a low-temperature technique, the tempering temperature of HSS is not reached, making it particularly well suited to TiN coating of HSS tools. As a result, heat treatment is not required following the PVD process. Koyilada et al. [ 46 ] used CVD and PVD-coated tools to investigate the machinability of Nimonic C-263. They found that PVD-coated tools exhibited higher hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, and toughness than CVD-coated tools.

sections.heading: Diffusion coatings
paragraphs: Low-carbon steels’ surface hardness can be improved by diffusing carbon or nitrogen into the surface to make them hardenable. The carbon-nitrogen-enriched surface hardens during heating and quenching, while the core stays robust. The surface can also be toughened via the ‘ion nitriding’ approach, which involves bombarding the steel surface with low-energy nitrogen ions generated in the plasma.

sections.heading: Ion-plantation
paragraphs: High-energy ions are used to penetrate the surface in this procedure. Nitrogen ions are the most widely employed cutting ions.

sections.heading: PVD and CVD multilayer coatings
paragraphs: Multilayer PVD and CVD coatings significantly enhance tool life and surface finish by reducing wear and thermal damage at high cutting speeds. PVD multilayer coatings (e.g., TiAlN/AlCrN) provide superior surface finish and tool life at high speeds due to their higher compressive strength and lower friction [ 71 ]. CVD multilayer coatings (e.g., Al 2 O 3 , TiCN) provide thicker, thermally stable layers that protect substrates under heavy mechanical loads. Nanocomposite and multilayer architectures further enhance wear resistance and thermal stability, which are critical in machining hard-to-cut superalloys such as Inconel and titanium alloys [ 72 ].

Nanocomposite coatings typically consist of nanocrystalline transition metal nitrides (e.g., TiN, CrN, TiAlN) embedded within an amorphous matrix such as Si 3 N 4 . A widely studied system is nc-TiN/a-Si 3 N 4 , where grain sizes are below 10 nm [ 7 ,  8 ]. The amorphous boundary phase suppresses grain growth and restricts dislocation motion, leading to exceptional hardness values exceeding 40–50 GPa.
The strengthening mechanisms include:
Hall–Petch strengthening due to grain refinement. Interface-controlled dislocation blocking. Spinodal decomposition in TiAlN systems. Residual compressive stress stabilization.

As reported by Musil [ 7 ], nanocomposite architectures significantly delay thermal softening and oxidation. Mayrhofer et al. [ 8 ] demonstrated that age hardening via spinodal decomposition in TiAlN enhances high-temperature hardness up to ~ 900–1000 °C. The amorphous matrix also restricts oxygen diffusion pathways, thereby improving oxidation resistance during dry high-speed machining.

sections.heading: Emerging surface treatment methods
paragraphs: Thermo reactive diffusion (TRD) and other environmental strategies are explored as cost-effective alternatives to traditional deposition, with TRD showing promising substrate adhesion and wear reduction in early studies [ 73 ].

sections.heading: Functional tool surface engineering
paragraphs: Recent research highlights the impact of micro-textured and engineered tool surfaces in improving chip control and heat dissipation, thereby enhancing both tool integrity and machining stability under dynamic loads [ 74 ]. Surface texturing has emerged as an effective functional surface-engineering strategy to enhance cutting-tool performance under dry, high-speed machining conditions. Micro- and nano-scale textures (such as dimples, grooves, and linear channels) fabricated using laser surface texturing or micro-machining techniques modify the tool–chip interface behaviour by reducing the real contact area between the chip and rake face. This reduction in contact area decreases frictional forces and limits adhesive wear. Additionally, textured surfaces act as micro-reservoirs for solid lubricants or for the entrapment of debris, promoting the formation of stable tribofilms and reducing material transfer from the workpiece to the tool. Controlled texture geometry further improves chip flow direction and reduces chip adhesion, thereby minimizing built-up edge (BUE) formation. Enhanced heat dissipation through interrupted contact zones also improves thermal stability. Recent studies [ 67 ,  68 ,  69 ,  70 ,  71 ,  72 ,  73 ,  74 ,  75 – 76 ] report significant reductions in flank wear and cutting forces when textured tools are used in dry machining of hardened steels and alloy materials, demonstrating their strong potential for sustainable and lubricant-free machining applications.

sections.heading: Fundamental wear mechanisms in cutting tools
paragraphs: Although tool life comparisons provide practical performance evaluation, a fundamental understanding of wear mechanisms is essential to explain cutting tool degradation under severe thermo-mechanical conditions. During machining, the tool–chip interface experiences extremely high contact pressures (1–3 GPa) and temperatures that may exceed 800–1000 °C depending on cutting speed and workpiece material. Under these conditions, complex tribological and thermochemical interactions govern tool failure. The dominant wear mechanisms include abrasive, adhesive, diffusion, and oxidative wear, which often operate simultaneously rather than independently [ 4 ,  5 – 6 ]. A mechanistic analysis of these degradation modes is critical for linking tool composition and coating architecture with performance.

sections.heading: Abrasive wear
paragraphs: Abrasive wear occurs when hard asperities, carbides, inclusions, or work-hardened phases in the workpiece plough or micro-cut the tool surface. This mechanism is particularly dominant during machining of hardened steels, cast irons, and metal matrix composites containing hard reinforcements [ 4 ,  5 ].
The resistance to abrasive wear is primarily governed by:
High hardness. Hot hardness retention. Microstructural stability.

Cemented carbides resist abrasion through hard WC grains embedded in a cobalt binder matrix. Grain refinement significantly reduces volumetric wear rate, as smaller carbide grains provide improved resistance to micro-fracture and pull-out [ 45 ].

Al 2 O 3 -based ceramics, CBN, and PCD tools exhibit superior abrasive wear resistance due to strong covalent bonding and extremely high hardness [ 9 ,  34 ]. CBN tools, in particular, maintain high hardness at elevated temperatures, making them highly effective in hard turning applications [ 30 ]. Thus, materials with strong covalent bonding (CBN, PCD, ceramics) and optimized carbide grain size (WC–Co) effectively mitigate abrasive wear.

sections.heading: Adhesive wear
paragraphs: Adhesive wear arises from localized welding at the tool–chip interface under high normal stresses and elevated temperatures. Repeated formation and rupture of adhesive junctions lead to material transfer, built-up edge (BUE) formation, and eventual edge chipping [ 4 ,  5 ].
Adhesive wear severity depends on:
Chemical affinity between tool and workpiece. Friction coefficient. Interfacial shear strength.

CBN exhibits a lower chemical affinity for ferrous materials than diamond, which reacts with iron at elevated temperatures [ 30 ]. This explains the superior performance of CBN over PCD in machining hardened steel. Coating technologies significantly mitigate adhesive wear. TiN, TiAlN, and multilayer PVD/CVD coatings reduce interfacial friction and suppress junction growth [ 24 ,  46 ]. Recent studies demonstrate that textured TiN–WS2–coated tools further reduce adhesive transfer under dry machining conditions by decreasing real contact area and forming stable tribo-films [ 59 ]. Therefore, alloying elements such as Al and Cr in coatings improve tribological behaviour by enhancing hardness and reducing chemical reactivity, thereby mitigating adhesion.

sections.heading: Diffusion wear
paragraphs: Diffusion wear becomes significant at elevated temperatures, particularly in high-speed machining of steels and nickel-based superalloys. Atomic migration occurs across the tool–chip interface due to concentration gradients and high thermal activation energy [ 4 ,  5 ].
For example:
Cobalt from WC–Co carbides may diffuse into the workpiece, weakening the binder phase. Carbon from diamond may dissolve into ferrous materials at high temperatures, accelerating crater wear.
This explains why PCD tools are unsuitable for ferrous machining despite their extreme hardness [ 10 ].

Al 2 O 3  layers deposited via CVD act as effective diffusion barriers, preventing atomic migration between tool and chip [ 62 ]. Similarly, CBN exhibits excellent chemical stability when machining hardened steels due to its low iron affinity [ 30 ]. Recent wear mechanism analysis of CBN tools during assisted turning further confirms that diffusion and chemical degradation accelerate crater wear at very high temperatures [ 60 ]. Thus, diffusion wear resistance is primarily governed by chemical stability and the presence of thermally stable barrier coatings.

sections.heading: Oxidative wear
paragraphs: Oxidative wear occurs when high-temperature exposure leads to tribo-chemical reactions between the tool material and atmospheric oxygen. Depending on the material system, oxide formation may be either protective or detrimental [ 6 ].

Coatings containing aluminium (e.g., TiAlN, AlCrN) form dense Al 2 O 3  scales at elevated temperatures, significantly improving oxidation resistance and thermal stability [ 71 ,  72 ]. Chromium additions promote the formation of Cr 2 O 3  layers, enhancing resistance to high-temperature degradation. Nanocomposite coatings further restrict oxygen diffusion pathways and improve oxidation stability through microstructural refinement [ 7 ,  73 ].
Therefore, alloying strategies that promote stable oxide formation significantly enhance high-temperature wear resistance in dry and high-speed machining environments.

sections.heading: Synergistic wear interactions
paragraphs: In practical machining operations, wear mechanisms rarely act independently. Diffusion may weaken the cobalt binder in WC–Co tools, making the tool more susceptible to abrasive grooving. Adhesive junction formation may initiate micro-cracks that propagate under mechanical stress, particularly in brittle ceramics and superhard tools [ 9 ,  34 ].
Hence, optimal cutting tool design requires a balanced combination of:

High hardness (abrasion resistance). Chemical stability (diffusion control). Low friction (adhesion control). Oxidation resistance (thermal stability). Adequate fracture toughness (resistance to chipping).

Modern multilayer and nanocomposite coatings are specifically engineered to mitigate multiple wear modes simultaneously through graded architectures and thermally stable phases [ 71 ,  72 ,  73 ,  74 – 75 ].

sections.heading: Intelligent tool systems
paragraphs: While integration of real-time monitoring and AI-driven adaptive control in cutting tools is still emerging, industry trends point to sensor-embedded tools that can track wear and optimize parameters in situ, aligning with digital manufacturing paradigms (Industry 4.0). Comparison between conventional and intelligent tool systems (Table  4 ) highlights the evolution from traditional machining to Industry 4.0-enabled smart machining systems.

sections.heading: Challenges and future directions
paragraphs: Key challenges include balancing hardness and toughness under extreme conditions, reducing reliance on environmentally harmful fluids, and developing innovative coatings that dynamically adapt to cutting conditions. Future research is expected to focus on:

sections.heading: Hybrid materials & additive manufacturing
paragraphs: Additively manufactured cutting tools allow complex internal cooling channels and tailored material gradients that were previously impossible, opening doors to new levels of performance and customization.

Additive manufacturing (AM) enables the fabrication of cutting tools with complex internal cooling channels and graded material architectures. However, significant metallurgical differences exist between AM-produced tools and those manufactured through conventional powder metallurgy (PM).

In laser-based AM processes, rapid solidification leads to fine cellular–dendritic microstructures with pronounced columnar grain growth along the build direction. This often results in crystallographic texture and microstructural anisotropy. Additionally, AM components may contain residual porosity arising from lack-of-fusion defects or gas entrapment, as well as residual tensile stresses generated by steep thermal gradients during layer-by-layer deposition. These features can influence fracture toughness and crack-propagation behaviour under cyclic cutting loads.

In contrast, PM-produced tools such as WC–Co carbides typically exhibit equiaxed carbide grains embedded in a uniformly distributed binder phase, with near-full densification achieved through liquid-phase sintering. The more homogeneous microstructure and lower residual stress levels contribute to predictable mechanical performance.

While AM introduces challenges related to porosity, anisotropy, and residual stress, it also enables microstructural tailoring and functional grading that are difficult to achieve through conventional PM routes [ 6 ,  71 ,  72 – 73 ]. A detailed understanding of these metallurgical distinctions is essential for reliable deployment of additively manufactured cutting tools in industrial applications.

sections.heading: Intelligent, sensor-integrated tools
paragraphs: Embedding sensor networks and coupling them with analytics and machine learning will enable tools that  self-optimize  cutting parameters in real time.

sections.heading: Balance between hardness & toughness
paragraphs: Developing coatings and tool materials that maintain extreme hardness without brittleness remains a key research focus—especially for interrupted cuts and hard turning applications [ 68 – 69 ].

sections.heading: Sustainable, low-impact manufacturing
paragraphs: Innovations that reduce reliance on harmful coolants and promote energy-efficient machining will shape future tool design criteria, driven by regulatory and ecological concerns.
These areas promise to improve machining efficiency, sustainability, and competitiveness in advanced manufacturing.

sections.heading: Industrial implications and practical guidance
paragraphs: From an industrial perspective, the selection of cutting tool materials plays a critical role in determining machining productivity, tool life, surface integrity, and overall manufacturing cost. For general-purpose machining of steels and cast irons, advanced coated cemented carbides offer an optimal balance between performance and cost, making them the most widely adopted solution in industry. In contrast, CBN tools are particularly suitable for hard turning of hardened steels, where high hot hardness and wear resistance are essential, while PCD tools are most effective for high-speed machining of non-ferrous and abrasive materials due to their superior hardness and thermal conductivity. However, the higher cost and brittleness of superhard materials necessitate their selective use in high-value or high-volume applications. Furthermore, integrating advanced surface coatings, micro-textured tool surfaces, and intelligent sensor-assisted tools offers practical pathways to enhance tool performance and extend tool life under demanding cutting conditions. Therefore, application-specific tool selection, taking into account workpiece material, machining parameters, and economic constraints, is essential for achieving sustainable, cost-effective manufacturing operations.

sections.heading: Economic considerations in tool material selection
paragraphs: Although super-hard materials such as CBN and PCD exhibit superior hot hardness and wear resistance, their significantly higher initial cost requires economic justification. Studies show that while CBN and PCD tools may cost several times as much as coated cemented carbides, their extended tool life and ability to operate at higher cutting speeds can reduce the overall cost per machined component, particularly in high-volume or high-value production environments [ 29 ,  30 ].

CBN tools are economically justified for hard turning hardened steels, where they replace grinding operations, improving productivity and dimensional accuracy [ 30 ]. Similarly, PCD tools are cost-effective for machining non-ferrous alloys and abrasive composites due to their exceptional wear resistance and low coefficient of friction [ 32 ,  33 – 34 ]. However, for general-purpose steel machining, advanced multilayer PVD/CVD-coated carbides often provide a more favourable balance between performance and cost [ 71 ,  74 ].
Therefore, optimal tool selection should consider not only hardness and wear resistance but also tool life, machining speed, production volume, and overall cost-per-part efficiency.

sections.heading: Artificial intelligence–based tool material selection frameworks
paragraphs: With the rapid advancement of Industry 4.0 and smart manufacturing, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly applied to cutting tool material selection and performance optimization. Traditional tool selection methods rely primarily on empirical guidelines and machining handbooks; however, AI-driven frameworks enable data-driven prediction of tool life, wear progression, and thermo-mechanical stability under varying cutting conditions.

Machine learning models such as artificial neural networks (ANN), support vector machines (SVM), random forest (RF), and deep learning architectures have been successfully applied to predict tool wear and surface roughness based on input variables including cutting speed, feed rate, depth of cut, coating type, and material composition [ 99 ,  100 – 101 ]. These models improve predictive accuracy and reduce reliance on costly trial-and-error experimentation.

In addition, multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) techniques integrated with AI algorithms facilitate optimal selection of tool materials by simultaneously considering hardness, fracture toughness, oxidation resistance, thermal conductivity, cost, and sustainability metrics [ 102 ]. Hybrid approaches combining genetic algorithms (GA) or particle swarm optimization (PSO) with ANN models enable simultaneous optimization of coating composition and machining parameters [ 103 ].

Recent studies also highlight the development of physics-informed machine learning frameworks, where material composition, microstructural descriptors, and thermo-mechanical properties are embedded into predictive models to improve generalization and interpretability [ 99 ,  104 ]. Such approaches are particularly relevant for nanocomposite coatings and additively manufactured tools, where compositional design strongly influences performance.

Furthermore, AI-based cost–performance modelling enables estimation of the cost per machined component by integrating tool life prediction with economic parameters, thereby enabling intelligent selection among coated carbides, CBN, and PCD tools based on production volume and machining severity [ 101 ,  103 ].

Therefore, AI-driven frameworks represent a transformative approach to tool material selection, linking composition, processing, microstructure, thermo-mechanical behavior, and economic performance into an integrated decision-support system.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The study acknowledges that cutting tool materials remain foundational to productivity, quality, and cost-effectiveness in metal-cutting processes. Ongoing advances in materials science and surface coating technologies have enabled the machining of complex, high-performance alloys with greater speed, accuracy, and durability. These developments not only extend tool life but also reduce manufacturing costs, improve resource utilisation, and enhance process sustainability. Despite these achievements, significant challenges persist—particularly in creating cost-efficient tools that maintain superior performance under extreme operating conditions. The next phase of innovation is likely to focus on hybrid tool materials, nano-engineered coatings, and intelligent cutting tools equipped with embedded sensors for real-time monitoring. Such advancements will be pivotal in addressing the evolving demands of high-precision, energy-efficient, and environmentally responsible manufacturing systems. A physics-based understanding of wear mechanisms enables more rational selection of tool materials and advanced coating design for sustainable, high-performance machining.
